title: The Evolution of Canaloplasty: Two Decades of Restoring and Reinforcing the Conventional Outflow Pathway
content: Surgery of Schlemm’s canal has evolved over two decades from bleb-dependent, ab-externo viscocanalostomy into a family of tissue-sparing, ab-interno, and scaffold-reinforced procedures. We trace five generations of canal surgery and evaluate whether durable structural reinforcement of the restored canal, with preservation of the trabecular meshwork, determines long-term outcome. Imaging and histology show that the glaucomatous canal is narrowed and partially collapsed, with canal area inversely related to intraocular pressure. Viscoelastic injected into the canal is cleared within 24 hours, whereas a tensioning suture sustains canal expansion beyond 20 months and outperforms viscocanalostomy, particularly at stringent pressure targets. Ab-interno canaloplasty sustains pressure and medication reduction for 3 to 6 years but leaves no structural element in the canal. A nitinol intracanalicular scaffold has 5-year randomized evidence of benefit but provokes persistent angle reactivity, with cumulative peripheral anterior synechiae of 14.6% versus 3.7% after cataract surgery alone. Acellular scleral allograft is safe and non-migrating as a uveoscleral cleft scaffold but has not been studied inside Schlemm’s canal. Biologic intracanalicular reinforcement is a coherent but untested next step that requires randomized, morphometric evaluation.
